value.overview: The Tropical Kingbird is a large, familiar flycatcher of open and semi-open habitats from the southern United States through Central America and much of South America. It often perches conspicuously on wires, fence posts, treetops, and other exposed places before making swift flights to catch insects. Its bright yellow underparts, gray head, brownish back, and dark tail make it one of the most recognizable flycatchers in tropical lowlands and towns.
value.classification: The Tropical Kingbird belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Tyrannus melancholicus.
value.identification: Adults have a gray head and throat, an olive or grayish breast, brown upperparts, dark wings and tail, and bright yellow lower underparts. The bill and legs are black. The bird is long-tailed and relatively large, with a slightly notched tail. Juveniles are duller, browner, and paler below. In Costa Rica, it may be confused with other yellow-bellied flycatchers, but its widespread occurrence, strong dark bill, gray head, and characteristic sharp, high-pitched calls are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America and across most of South America. In Costa Rica, it is an abundant resident found throughout the country, from the lowlands to about 1,850 meters and less commonly to approximately 2,400 meters. It uses savannas, pastures, agricultural land, river margins, scrub, gardens, roadsides, forest edges, and urban and suburban areas. It generally avoids deep, closed forest and favors open places with scattered perches.
value.migrationStatus: Most Tropical Kingbirds are resident, including the abundant Costa Rican population. Birds at the northern and southern extremes of the range can migrate seasonally, but Costa Rica is primarily occupied year-round rather than serving mainly as a wintering area for this species.
value.breeding: Breeding commonly occurs in open or semi-open landscapes with trees and shrubs. The female builds a shallow, loosely woven cup from dry grasses, stems, vines, and other plant fibers, usually in an exposed position in a tree or shrub. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported mainly from March through July. Clutches usually contain two or three pale eggs with darker markings, and incubation lasts about 15 days. Both adults feed the young after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: The Tropical Kingbird feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, bees, wasps, termites, butterflies, moths, dragonflies, and grasshoppers. It usually hunts from an exposed perch, launching into the air to capture prey in flight. It may also hover briefly to take insects from vegetation. Fruits and berries supplement the diet, especially when insect prey is less available, and the species can forage successfully in gardens, farms, towns, and other disturbed habitats.
value.behavior: This kingbird is usually seen alone or in pairs, often sitting upright on a conspicuous perch and repeatedly making sallies after insects. It is territorial around a nest and may aggressively chase birds that approach too closely, including other flycatchers and larger species. Its calls are sharp, high-pitched twitters, and males may give more elaborate vocalizations around dawn. Pairs may remain together throughout the year in areas where the species is resident, such as Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliable current global trend is stated here; the species remains widespread, common, and adaptable across much of its range.
